name: Copán
info: Copán is an archaeological site of the Maya civilization in the Copán Department of western Honduras, occupied for more than two thousand years and the capital of a major Classic period kingdom from the 5th to the 9th century CE.

facts.founded: The first known stone architecture in the valley dates to about the 9th century BCE; the city was refounded in 426 CE by K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', who established a new Maya kingdom and royal dynasty.
facts.where: In the alluvial basin of the Copán River, a fertile mountain valley among foothills in western Honduras, not far from the border with Guatemala.
facts.known: The dynasty of sixteen kings founded in 426; the Acropolis and its tombs; the Hieroglyphic Stairway with about 2,200 glyphs; Altar Q; the Rosalila temple; the carved stelae; the defeat by Quiriguá in 738
facts.today: Copán is an archaeological site, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, 1.6 kilometres from the village of Copán Ruinas.

t: Copán was occupied from the Early Preclassic period to the Postclassic, and in 426 CE K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' refounded it as the capital of a new Maya kingdom whose dynasty ruled for four centuries.
Its king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil raised the city to its height and ranked it among the four most powerful Maya states, but he was captured and beheaded by the king of Quiriguá in 738.
The dynasty ended in the early 9th century amid overpopulation and disease, the ceremonial centre was abandoned by the early 10th century, and archaeologists have worked there since the 19th century.
dyk: The Hieroglyphic Stairway of Copán takes its name from some 2,200 glyphs that together form the longest known Maya hieroglyphic text, which is still being reconstructed because the glyphic blocks were scrambled when the temple's façade collapsed.
ev: The first known stone architecture is built in the Copán valley
K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' is installed as king and refounds the city as the capital of a new kingdom
Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil is captured by the king of Quiriguá and beheaded
Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat dedicates Altar Q, which shows the first sixteen kings of the dynasty
Ukit Took' comes to the throne, and his Altar L is left unfinished
Diego García de Palacio writes to Philip II of Spain with the first post-conquest mention of Copán
John Lloyd Stephens publishes his description of Copán with Frederick Catherwood's drawings
The Carnegie Institution diverts the Copán River southwards to protect the Acropolis

sections.origins:
Copán lies in the alluvial basin of the Copán River, a fertile and well-watered mountain valley in western Honduras, not far from the border with Guatemala. It was occupied for more than two thousand years, from the Early Preclassic period to the Postclassic. In the Preclassic the valley floor was undulating, swampy and prone to seasonal flooding, and the valley was long a place of agriculture before the first known stone architecture was built there about the 9th century BCE. In the Early Classic its inhabitants flattened the valley floor and carried out building projects to protect the city's architecture from floods.

The city's early history is hard to read. Later texts mention its predynastic rulers, but none of them predates the refounding of the city in 426 CE. One inscription refers to the year 321 BCE, though no text explains it, and another links an event at Copán to one 208 days earlier, in 159 CE, at an unknown place, possibly El Mirador. Archaeologists have found that the first monumental structures under the Acropolis date to the early 5th century CE, when K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' established the royal dynasty, and that they were built on earlier earth and cobble structures of the predynastic period. The ancient name of the city was probably Oxwitik, "Three Witiks", although the meaning of witik is obscure.
sections.growth:
In 426 CE the city was refounded by K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' as the capital of a new Maya kingdom. His son, K'inich Popol Hol, redesigned the core of the city and built the first version of its ballcourt. Copán became one of the more powerful Maya city states and a regional power in the southern Maya area. Its position in the valley let it act as a trade hub between the Maya lowlands and the non-Maya peoples of southern Central America, and it controlled access to the upper Motagua River valley, a source of jadeite and obsidian. It also influenced centres across western and central Honduras and introduced Mesoamerican traits to their local elites.

Under K'ak' Chan Yopaat, who was crowned in 578, the population rose and housing spread over all the available land of the valley. The apogee of Copán's achievements came under Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil, who was crowned in July 695. During his reign the city's sculpture developed into the full in-the-round style characteristic of Copán, and on Stela A, raised in 731, he ranked his city with Tikal, Calakmul and Palenque as one of the four most powerful states of the Maya region. At the peak of its power in the Late Classic the kingdom had a population of at least 20,000 and covered over 250 square kilometres. One estimate gives 18,000 to 25,000 people in the valley, of whom 6,000 to 9,000 lived in central Copán.
sections.rulers:
Little is known of Copán's rulers before 426 CE. In that year a warrior named K'uk' Mo' Ajaw was installed on the throne and given the royal name K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo'. He was probably from Tikal and was likely sponsored by Siyaj Chan K'awiil II of Tikal, and indirect evidence suggests that he took the city by military means. On Altar Q he is shown as a Teotihuacano warrior. In 1995 a tomb under the Hunal temple was found to hold the skeleton of an elderly man with battle wounds, identified as his, whose bones show him to have been foreign to Copán. The city stayed closely allied with Tikal. The dynasty he founded ruled for four centuries and included sixteen kings plus a probable pretender. Among them B'alam Nehn was ruling by 504, Moon Jaguar was enthroned in May 553 and K'ak' Chan Yopaat in 578. Smoke Imix, who ruled from 628 to 695, is thought to have reigned longest.

Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil installed K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat as a vassal on the throne of Quiriguá in 724. In April 738 the Quiriguá king captured him, and six days later he was decapitated there. K'ak' Joplaj Chan K'awiil became the 14th ruler on 7 June 738 and died in January 749. K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil followed him, and Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat, whose mother was a noblewoman of Palenque, took the throne in June 763. Ukit Took' came to the throne on 6 February 822.
sections.life:
The core of the city was the Main Group, an area of 600 by 300 metres. Its Acropolis was the raised royal complex at the heart of Copán, with two plazas called the West Court and the East Court, and to the north lay the Hieroglyphic Stairway, the ballcourt and the Monument Plaza, which holds the greatest concentration of sculpted monuments. The third ballcourt, built under Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil, was one of the largest of the Classic period and carried 16 mosaic sculptures of macaws. The city developed a distinctive sculptural style within the lowland Maya tradition, perhaps to emphasise the Maya ethnicity of its rulers. A causeway, or sacbe, linked the Main Group to the Sepulturas Group, which was mostly elite residences with stone benches, some carved, and tombs.

Central Copán had a density of 1,449 structures per square kilometre. By 800 CE the Sepulturas Group consisted of about 50 buildings around seven courtyards, and its most important building was the House of the Bakabs, the palace of a powerful nobleman of the time of Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat. A part of the group was a subdistrict occupied by non-Maya people from Central Honduras who took part in the trade network that brought in goods from that region. In the later 8th century the nobility grew more powerful and built palaces with hieroglyphic benches as richly made as the king's. Deforestation of the valley meant that firewood could no longer be spared to burn limestone to plaster, and the Rosalila temple was the last building there with such elaborate stucco decoration.
sections.crises:
The worst political disaster of Copán's history came in 738, when Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil was captured and beheaded by his former vassal, K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quiriguá, who had allied himself with Calakmul. The exact details are unknown. There is no evidence that either city was attacked, and it seems the Quiriguá king ambushed him. Copán did not retaliate. Major construction ceased and no new monuments were raised for the next 17 years, the city lost the Motagua River trade route to Quiriguá, and it may even have been subject to its former vassal. Under K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil a programme of renewal began, and rulers again built monumental structures within a few decades.

By the end of the reign of Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat the city was struggling with overpopulation and a lack of local resources, and living standards had fallen. Its population was over 20,000, and it had long needed to import basic necessities. In 810 the king took part in the k'atun-ending ceremony at Quiriguá, not at Copán. His funerary shrine shows the king performing war dances, and a column from it has a text reading "toppling of the Foundation House" that may refer to the fall of the dynasty. Shortage and disease afflicted the valley when Ukit Took' came to the throne, and even the nobility were struck. The collapse of the city-state, thought to have occurred between 800 and 830, was sudden. The population then fell from perhaps over 20,000 to less than 5,000, though people in the valley continued to live there.
sections.legacy:
After the end of the dynasty the area continued to be occupied, and in the Postclassic period villagers took stone from the monumental buildings to make house platforms. Only a few farming hamlets stood in the valley when the Spanish arrived in the 16th century. The first mention after the Spanish conquest is a letter of 8 March 1576 from Diego García de Palacio to Philip II. Jean-Frédéric Waldeck drew the ruins for a month in the early 19th century, Colonel Juan Galindo led an expedition there in 1834, and John Lloyd Stephens and Frederick Catherwood visited and published a description with drawings in 1841. Alfred Maudslay later visited, and expeditions sponsored by the Peabody Museum of Harvard University worked there, among them the excavation of the Hieroglyphic Stairway in 1892 and 1893. The Carnegie Institution also sponsored work in conjunction with the government of Honduras.

The Copán River had gradually changed course and cut away the eastern part of the Acropolis, leaving a cross-section 37 metres high at its tallest and 300 metres long. The Carnegie Institution diverted the river southwards in the 1930s to protect the site. UNESCO declared Copán a World Heritage Site in 1980, and the Honduran government designated it a cultural monument in 1982. The monument covers 66 hectares, and looting remains a threat to it. A life-size copy of the Rosalila building stands at the site museum.

summary: Copán, in the Copán valley of western Honduras, was refounded in 426 CE as the capital of a Maya kingdom that grew into a regional power. Its king was beheaded by Quiriguá in 738, the dynasty ended in the early 9th century and the ceremonial centre was abandoned by the early 10th century.
notes: START/END: the article says the first known stone architecture dates to about the 9th century BC and that the city was abandoned in the early 10th century; I used -900 and 900, both circa. It also says occupation began in the Early Preclassic without a year, and the city was refounded in 426.
ELEVATION: the article gives 600 metres in one paragraph and 700 metres in another; left out.

LAST KING: the History section calls Ukit Took' the last known king, but the Structure 10L-11 and 10L-18 passages call Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat the last known king; the dynasty is also described as sixteen kings plus a probable pretender who would have been seventeenth. I did not say who was last. Ukit Took' is not named in the text above as last; the editor may wish to check.

COLLAPSE: the article says the collapse of the city-state is thought to have occurred between 800 and 830 and was sudden, yet that the population persisted and even flourished between 750 and 900 and then gradually declined, and that the decrease took over four centuries to show signs of collapse. I gave the 800 to 830 date as 'thought' and the fall in population without a year. The fall from over 20,000 to under 5,000 is given by the article for the 8th and 9th centuries.
POPULATION: 'at least 20,000' for the kingdom and 18,000 to 25,000 for the valley are both in the article; I gave both, as it does. The ranges 6,000-9,000 for central Copán are as given.

The article's section 'Recent Archaeological Discoveries and Interpretation (2010-2024)' (a 'Scribe King' burial of 2012; LiDAR mapping of over 6,000 structures) cites nothing and I left it out as it could not be checked against the other parts of the article.
Altar Q: the article says it shows 16 kings; Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat is the 16th; it was dedicated in 776. The founding date of the dynasty is given as 426, and 426-427 in the Altar Q text; I used 426.
Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil's capture is dated April 738 and his decapitation six days later; Stela A is dated 731; the ballcourt's completion date is given as 6 January 738.
'Rediscovery' appears in the article's text; I did not use it. I wrote only who visited, drew, described and excavated the site, and gave the 1576 letter as the first post-conquest mention.

Left out for space: the Motmot capstone, the Xukpi stone, Tomb of the 'Lady in Red', the individual stelae, the tombs of Smoke Imix and others, the 'Sub-Jaguar' tomb, Tatiana Proskouriakoff's reading of Altar Q, UNESCO funding figures, the Cemetery and North groups.
The Motagua trade route: the article says Copán 'controlled access to the upper Motagua River valley' and later that Quiriguá took the 'key Motagua River trade route'.
